# Summary of Alfred North Whitehead
Alfred North Whitehead (1861–1947) was an English mathematician, logician, philosopher, and educator, renowned for his extensive contributions to mathematics, logic, metaphysics, and education. He was educated at Sherborne and Trinity College, Cambridge, where he studied mathematics under Edward Routh and graduated as fourth wrangler. Whitehead taught mathematics and physics at Cambridge, collaborating closely with Bertrand Russell on the monumental three-volume *Principia Mathematica* (1910–13), a foundational work in mathematical logic. Later, he transitioned to philosophy and became a prominent metaphysician, moving to Harvard University in 1924 where he produced key philosophical works including *Science and the Modern World* (1925) and *Process and Reality* (1929). His metaphysics, known as "process philosophy," emphasized events and relations over static matter, positing a universe of interrelated experiential processes and introducing the concept of "prehension" as a form of perception extending beyond conscious beings.
Whitehead notably critiqued Cartesian dualism and scientific materialism, proposing that reality consists of overlapping events rather than enduring substances and emphasizing creativity and relationality. His philosophical views incorporated a novel conception of God as a dipolar entity engaged dynamically with the world. Besides his philosophical legacy, Whitehead was deeply involved in educational reform, advocating for an imaginative, transdisciplinary approach opposing rote learning of "inert ideas." His influence spans theology, ecology, physics, and organizational theory, with institutions and projects dedicated to his work, notably the Whitehead Research Project. Despite the complexity and difficulty of his writings, Whitehead remains a significant figure whose ideas continue to inspire diverse scholarly fields.
